definition: Sycophant means a person who flatters others for personal gain.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sycophant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sycophant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Every remark the heiress made at dinner was instantly the cleverest thing the table had ever heard — she traveled, her butler observed, with a full set of sycophants.
An admirer sits far below a sycophant — admiration can be silent, sincere, and want nothing at all.
Flatterer stops short of sycophant: a flatterer overpraises, perhaps just to be liked, while a sycophant runs flattery as a business aimed at the powerful.

Bootlicker is the schoolyard insult for the sycophant — the same creature, cruder name. A bootlicker grovels openly to whoever holds power over him, and the word drips contempt. Sycophant says the same thing in a suit, polished enough for reviews, histories, and courtrooms.

A yes-man works one narrow trade: agreeing with every word the boss says, whatever he privately thinks. A sycophant runs a wider business — compliments, favors, and flattery aimed anywhere up the ladder, always priced for a return. Every yes-man is a sycophant; the reverse is not guaranteed.

A toady attaches himself to one important person and fawns in close attendance — running errands, laughing first, agreeing loudest. Sycophant is the broader, more formal word for anyone who flatters for personal gain; toady adds the picture of eager, hovering servility at a particular patron's elbow.

Sycophant is the polished insult — reviews, histories, and courtrooms use it where bootlicker would be too crude, and it always implies the flattery is a strategy aimed at the powerful.
Blandish, in this unit, is the sycophant's verb of trade; a flatterer without an agenda deserves the milder word.

The month Dana Reyes was named chief executive, her jokes got funnier.
Colleagues who had dozed through her budget briefings now took notes on her weekend anecdotes; her worst idea in years — the mango-themed rebrand — was called visionary in three separate meetings.

Her predecessor warned her that a corner office breeds sycophants, and told her how he had counted his: praise that arrives before the idea is finished, agreement that grows louder as the stock rises, kindness that always precedes a request.
Dana started keeping the tally herself.
The week she announced her retirement, four of her most devoted admirers discovered other lunch plans, and the mango rebrand was quietly declared a mistake — by its loudest former champions.
